utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, yesterday when we had no transcript, this is an audio, but I think there is no need to have this all transcribed because nothing of any substance was dealt with, apart from one thing, that is that the Prosecution expressed its preference for housekeeping matters to be dealt with immediately after the conclusion of the testimony of Mr. Konings. So that is now on the record. Mr. Konings, I would like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the begging of your testimony, that is that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Colonel, just before we begin, I'd just like to ask you, are you familiar with the acronym --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think know we have slight problems with the screens, but I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Colonel, with the acronym the MEETC, M-e-e-t-c, being mission: The E been enemy; T being terrain and weather; next T being troops and support available; the TC, the T being time available; and the C civil consideration. Are you familiar with that acronym as an acronym for a short-hand version of a way a commander would assess a battle situation and what he wants to do?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not use the word familiar because we use a slightly different system, but I exactly know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. So you -- maybe in the Dutch system they would use different initials but the concept is basically the same?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So we might talk about it in a little bit and to the extent the concept is different please advise me and we can go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we go into some of this, I did hand out those two documents yesterday. I do believe it may be expeditious to provide Colonel Konings with those two copies because it will allow us to move things a bit more quickly. Mr. President, should I proceed or wait for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If everyone has --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, no that will be fixed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, looking at your report you do take issue at some points about the methodology and logic of attacking Knin, but before we get into the specifics the Knin I'd just like to talk to you about some concepts about attacks in general and the NATO philosophy on that. So that will the first topic before moving from the macro to the micro before we move down to Knin itself. And just addressing your attention to land operations as a whole you would agree, would you not, that the purpose of land combat is not necessarily destruction of the enemy forces but you want to force capitulation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. There can be many, many objects that you want to achieve through a land operation. We call that the end state that you want to achieve and the end state that you want to achieve doesn't necessarily mean capitulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you're saying in some sense you want total destruction of the enemy and maybe in other cases you would just want capitulation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that is not what I'm saying. There are various opportunities or various objectives in between. What we try to do is a land operation is working on -- to influence the will and capabilities and the understanding of an opponent. That's what we try to do, and if that takes in certain moments or on certain places the use of violence, of military violence, then you have to do so. And if that means that you have to destroy certain parts of the society or of the military capabilities of the -- I should not say society but of the military capabilities of an opponent then you have to do so. But you have to remind that you have to reach such an end state as is formulated to you by the political -- by your own government or a coalition, political coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pursuant to rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there will always be rules of engagement but the end state is not necessarily capitulation or destruction the end state can be that an operation leads to a peace agreement between two parties. Doesn't need to be, necessarily, two states; it can be a conflict in a country where a piece enforcing or peacekeeping force is established by the international community and such a peace force is a military operation as well. I additionally I should say that in NATO and also in the Netherlands army we do not make any difference anymore between combat operations or between offensive operations or between defensive operations. An operation is an operation, and it doesn't matter in which context it is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn if we can to a bit of a discussion on NATO concepts and I would like to direct your attention, Colonel, to 1D65-0227. That is the I believe the hard copy there is the allied joint document for land operations AJP 3.2. I believe you have that in front of you. And I'd first like to just expand on your last several answers when we talk about an operations, and I want to direct your attention to section 204 on the first page after that document, if we could. Towards the bottom of that page and if we could just look at that: "Land combat is a fundamentally human endeavour, and human building decide rationally or irrationally when they are beaten. Historically, the defeat of an enemy force has almost never come at the point of a 100 percent loss to the loser. It normally occurs at some earlier point which depends on the losers' will and cohesion. On an individual or small unit level, emotions, such as fear, panic, shock, and surprise are significant. These emotions adversely affect decision- making in commanders. When an enemy feels is he beaten, he withdraws his participation from the battle or engagement." If you can turn to the next page, top of the page, second full sentence in, actually it's the third full sentence in, "The collective ...": "The collective withdrawal of an enemy's participation in battle is primarily a mental rather than a physical issue and may not be rational." Now, I think you touched on some of the concepts just a bit certainly in a part of your answer, sir, about land concept. But you would agree that that is an approach that you want to take in assuming you're in land, combat and you're in facing an opposition that you try to -- or you know that emotion such as fear, panic, shock and surprise are very significant to your opponent, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to re-read what you said because I'm not quite sure I understand your directed question to me. Can you rephrase it because I don't know where you're aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It may have been a terrible question, Colonel, and I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies to the reporter at quarter after 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You would agree fundamentally that in land operations that emotions such as fear, panic, shock, and surprise are very significant and oft-times they effect the decision making in a commander?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are certainly very important aspects in a land operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And taking this one step further in a land operation, and going back to the last sentence, generally the withdrawal of an enemy is because primarily -- of a mental breakdown, as opposed to a purely physical breakdown; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is a combination. It can be a combination of both -- well, as I say it's probably a combination of both, but no situation will be the same. A mental break down can be caused by threatening of a force. If you as a country or as a coalition are able to show the force that you have and that you have a certain -- not a certain, but a full willingness to apply that force if necessary it may already change the mental state -- the mental -- the mental position of a state or a party or a country in such a way that they even don't dream about using their own armed forces against a -- a -- a force that attacks them or that wants to enter their country as an intervening force because it is not only about attacking forces when you talk about applying violence, it is also talking about forces that are established by the international community to intervene in any conflict as we have had numerous examples in the past. So the mental position of a party of an army of a government is a very important one, and I -- I had not deny that they will not by influence by things like panic, shock, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And to -- to take that one step further, Colonel, as a commander you would want to encourage that mental break down by your enemy, wouldn't you, as a means of achieving your goals?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the possibilities that have you that you work on a mental breakdown of enemy forces or opposition forces or even a whole of society by working through the way of what we discussed yesterday information operations to work on the hearts and minds of a population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us -- if we may stay on this page and just move down to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just scroll up just a bit. Thank you, and we talk about the manoeuvrist approach in paragraph 207: "The manoeuvrist approach is one in which shattering the enemy's overall cohesion and will to fight rather than his materiel is paramount." Now, likewise you're familiar with this concept as well, are you not.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we just talk about taking that issue concerning the overall cohesion and then just take it back to yet another UN [sic] document in D1247. Again, this is the allied joint doctrine, AJP-01. And if we can go to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It -- on transcript it reads UN document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: NATO document, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page and the attack on the adversary's will and cohesion. I'm sorry, if I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D65-0212, which is part of D1247. This is ... under the rubric of attacking the adversary's will and cohesion. It notes that: "All attacks against an adversary must comply with" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What page are we.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm looking at page -- in the hard copy it's 4-11, in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the top of that page: "All attacks against an adversary must comply with international law; in particular, attacks may only be made against military objectives. The decisive element of a campaign will usually involve some form of offensive action against the will cohesion of adversaries." Now that is generally standard NATO doctrine about an offensive action that incorporates some form of attack against the will and cohesion of your enemy; is that not correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it exactly meant as it is written so I have nothing to add to that. It says perfectly clear it involves some form of offensive action against the will an cohesion, so I don't see the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to go to the next point and maybe we can make that purpose. In attacking the will cohesion of your enemy, NATO doctrine, and under NATO doctrine -- in inducing shock in your enemy is an effective means of breaking the will cohesion of your enemy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you now step from offensive action to one of the possibilities which is shock but offensive action is much more. I have to remind you that when we write here, "offensive action" that incorporates everything, especially including the use of non-lethal means, so offensive action means also the use of psychological actions that's what we mean about by offensive actions. When we talk in this document about attacking the will and understanding or influencing then we incorporate every mean that is -- that a coalition has available, and the mistake that people quite often make is that when you read the word offensive action they immediately think on the term iron against iron, or in other words the use of armoured vehicles and fighting soldiers against other armoured vehicles and armoured soldiers. That is definitely not the red tape in this document. This document describes the whole of capabilities that a coalition has in order to enter a conflict and to bring that conflict the end state that is described by the political committee of the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one of the ways just taking what you said, Colonel, to -- to destroy the will and cohesion through your adversaries is a shock action, a shock action by -- in this case the HV against the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not -- I have been asked yesterday not to repeat myself by the President. I can only repeat that what you say, every -- every action that you can use is of course possible. So shock is one of the possibilities, and I will not deny that destruction of enemy targets is also one of the opportunities, is also one of the possibilities. So we should not -- we should be very precise in that. An army, a coalition force has all the means given them by the political community available to use violence, if necessary, but it should be -- it should be proportional and it should be in the way, it should be legal. That's the whole -- the whole point. And I have to add that, if you are able to use other means than violence in reaching the end state, and even if it takes lives of your own side and even if it takes a longer period then that could be your priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what you just said is the doctrine of the Dutch army. It is not necessarily a reflection of the law on armed conflict is it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that that is the reflection of the laws of armed conflict. It is it the reflection of what we have on the screen here and it's the reflection of what we have described in -- in the Netherlands doctrine as well. But I can assure you that the reflection that I gave you just before and the way how we have to inter -- how we have to read the document as it is in front of you, because I do think it's quite difficult to take out certain parts, and I understand fully why you are doing that and focus on certain elements, the whole background of this document is, that it is all about lethal and especially non-lethal use of military means and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I intervene for a second. From your question, Mr. Kehoe, I understood that you'd like to know from the witness whether achieving a shock effect would be excluded from legitimate means in combat operation or in -- in this type of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turned the other way, using shock effect is a legitimate means in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, that may cause the problem. Of course, a shock effect is an effect and I think what the witness told us that it depends on the means used to achieve such a shock effect. I mean that is not difficult to understand. But let's then put it in clear terms to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is achieving a shock effect by whatever means always legitimate, Mr. Konings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think if you use -- let's put it in a way that shock effects are not only purely destruction is also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking: Is shock effects achieved by whatever means under all circumstances legitimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it is aimed against a military target and if it's done with the -- the military means that are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying if, if, if; so it is not under all circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not under all circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is it a clear answer. Now, I understand this from your previous answer, to seek to achieve a shock effect it may well be within the legitimate means, yes, of operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed with this line of questioning on this document, I'd just offer into evidence 1D65-0227.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D1254 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And using - thank you, Mr. President - D1254, if we could turn to page 204 in that document, where we talk a little bit about shock. And that is 1D65 -- the page is 1D65-0231. And it's under the rubric of attacking the enemy's understanding will and cohesion, and I'd just like to go through a few concepts with you to explain this a bit further, Colonel, and ask your assistance in this matter. In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe -- you say page 2 out of 4 but the numbering is different. It starts with 2 out of 1 out of 1, 2 out of -- 2-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2-4, yes, that is the 4th page -- under what section you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 0215, towards the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 0215, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes: "When an army fights it should seek to attack the enemy's understanding, will and cohesion. To direct attacks effectively requires understanding the enemy, his system, ... his motivation. Whenever possible a commander should attack his enemy systemically. Doing so" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it reads systemically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, systemically, apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Doing so should leave it unable to respond effectively as the situation develops. One ... way of achieving this is through ... shock of which the classic symptoms are numbness and irrational behaviour." If we could just move down to the next paragraph, 0216, three sentences -- three sentences in, five line. "The tactical effects of shock may be perceived as local panic or collapse." If we could turn your attention before I go into this with a question for you, back to D1247, the allied joint doctrine, AJP-01, and I turn to paragraph 425, which is -- again back of 4-11, and it's 1D65-0212. And 425 subdivision a (2): "In the physical sense, the psychological effect may be so great as to render fighting unnecessary." So, Colonel, just in layman's terms when you go through a shock action and we'll go through exactly what that is, the goal, of course, is to -- as the doctrine reads, to numb, infuse the enemy with some degree of numbness or irrational behaviour and to break down the enemy psychologically to essentially render fighting unnecessary. Is that not one of the goals that NATO has of using shock methods against your enemy?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clearly describes here that a possibility to use inside your operation is to make use of shock action, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one of the days to induce shock is through artillery fire; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that artillery fire is -- is a possibility to bring in shock, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us back to a little bit more of a sophisticated description of a shock action according to the NATO doctrine that we have in D1257. 1254, excuse me, D1254. And turning to two out of five, 2-5, which is 1D65-0232, in paragraph 221, describing the shock action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just scroll down this a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Under shock action, 0221: "Shock action is a sudden, concentrated application of violence. Shock action numbs, deters, and frightens. At the collective level ... by concentrations of fire and indirect fire and a high tempo of advanced [sic] employing closely coordinated fire and manoeuvre." If we can turn just continue on before we go in here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe you read advanced employing there. I read, "A high tempo of advance employing closely coordinated ..." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did I misread that, Judge? If I did, I apologise. "High tempo of advance employing closely coordinated fire and manoeuvre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, due to overlapping speakers, I'd like to repeat what I said, is that you read "advanced" where I read, "A high tempo of advance employing closely coordinated," et cetera. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page and look at 0223, that's two of six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First sentence there: "Shock effects can at times be observed as collapse. Collapse may be either progressive or catastrophic." If we go to the last sentence of that paragraph without reading it all: "Panic is a major indicator of catastrophic collapse ... is infectious and is transmitted as much by rumour as by fact. Since bad news travels fast perception of failure is the best mechanism to promote actual failure." Now if we can just turn one more page to two of seven, 0226 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You apparently insist on saying two of seven where it is seven in section 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now it is it approximately the third or the fourth time so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll do my best to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, attacks on understanding will and cohesion can be carried out by seizing and retaining the initiative pre-emption, location, and disruption. I'm getting a bit ahead of myself. Let's just -- before I go into that. Before we go into dislocation and disruption. Going back to the actual shock aspect and incorporating this, one of the significant by-products of the shock action and in causing the collapse is inducing panic in your adversary to assist the -- in the demise of your adversary as quickly as possible. Is that an accurate assessment of NATO doctrine?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the many ways that is described here in this doctrine document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going yet further in the ways of that attack, and I got ahead of myself a bit, talking about dislocation and disruption and let's just talk about those concepts. What is a dislocation and disruption? What are we talking about in a military context? And maybe I can just help you out if we go down to 229 --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's okay. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I've been the co-writer of this document so I know where to find my text. And it just clearly says that: "Dislocation is to dislocate the enemy, is to deny him the ability to bring his strengths to bear, thus preventing him from fighting on his terms. His purpose is wider than the frustration of the enemy plan. It seeks to render his strengths irrelevantly by avoiding them or fixing them so that they are ineffective. It may be deliberate or [indiscernible] of other actions and deep penetration and envelopment are two mechanisms of dislocation." So that's what you try to do. You try to cut off elements. You try to dislocate - as it says - enemy elements so that there -- you try to break his complete organisation. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, on that score you just noted that you are one of the co-writers of it this document. Can you explain that just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been involved in a writing team that has been writing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or have I been a member of a writing team that was writing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would that be the whole document or just -- the whole document?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So are you very familiar with these concepts?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with these concepts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And staying on what you just read, one of the methods of attack is deep penetration and envelopment, do you see that you just read that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are methods of dislocation, what are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean deputy penetration?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or envelopment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deep penetration can be done in many ways. It can be done by sending out a force on the ground and trying to penetrate deep in the enemy territory in order seize a very important element in that territory. For example, a headquarter or important persons, but you can do that also by -- by air. You can send in air mobile forces, you can parachute troops, so that they're all means trying to dislocate enemy forces that's the way you bring -- that's the way that you bring in a disorganisation of his defence, his attacking forces in depth, whatever is happening in that scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying with the comment that you made about in depth, the dislocation in depth is well inside the front line area. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't mean -- no. Depth did no given distance in that. Depth can even mean depth in time. So there is no -- no -- no cypher connected to the word depth. Depth can be -- well there is no cypher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not accurate enough. We're talking about in depth you also would consider an attack in depth well inside of the enemy lines towards facilities that might support the enemy that might not be at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I mean with in depth that. Deep operations are operations that can be on a certain distance from the territory where you are in, for example, close combat with your enemy and then you talk about actions that may dislocate reserve forces that may dislocate supporting forces, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit more about fixing the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move on this document to 0307 on pages 3-3, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying with this first sentence: "To fix the enemy is to deny the enemy his goals, to distract him, and thus deprive him of his freedom of action." So taking this sequentially, sir, one of the considerations that NATO has doctrine on is the use of a shock action sometimes at well beyond, well inside enemy lines to fix the enemy, distract him, confuse him and deprive him of his freedom of action; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite certain that shock actions will be used to fix him, because fixing the enemy -- shock action is as we have seen before is something of a concentrated use of violence during a short period, while fixing the enemy and taking away his freedom of movement, his freedom of action may take much longer time. And I do not think that shock action is the things we would use in order to fix an enemy because shock action is short, quick, heavy, and brings in panic, chaos on that moment, while fixing an enemy is something of a long breath. You fix an enemy for a long-term so that you concentrate -- that you force him, that you do not allow him to move his forces in that area. So that takes a long time. That is not coming from one minute to the other. So I had not directly connect shock action to the possibility of fixing the enemy, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand your thinking on this Colonel but just let's take this one step further. Would you agree, sir, that during a shock action you could very well simultaneously fix the movements of your enemy, could you not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not meant here in the concept of fixing the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand I'm asking you that question.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once are you in contact with an enemy, of course, you fix that element of the enemy when a platoon of infantry is in direct combat with an enemy force, you fix that enemy, you fix your own force. But what is meant to be here is on a large-scale. You don't have to -- we should realise that this document describes the operational level, describes not the lower levels. This describes an operation as a whole. So one of the things you can do in your operation is to fix important elements of the enemy, and it is not meant to be by -- by a short moment in time or a one-short action because then you do not fix the enemy. You fix the enemy only on that spot. What is meant here is that you fix the larger portion of an enemy force for a longer period so that you are able to manoeuvre with your own complete force around it to achieve your objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you're talking about fixing, you're talking about in a sense of artillery you can use artillery to fix the enemy over a course of time, a day or days depending on how long you wanted to fix them?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot. You definitely cannot fix an enemy force by artillery alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not saying artillery alone, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying artillery alone but artillery and other aspects and if I said that, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read here: "You can use artillery to fix the enemy over a course of time or day or days depending ..." so you did not enter any other force as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I stand corrected, Colonel, and we just take that a little further. Artillery in conjunction with other forces can be used to fix the enemy over the course of time be it a day, two days.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery is always part of a manoeuvre force so if you talk about fixing an enemy that is done by a manoeuvre force that includes all weapon systems -- so including artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let's talk a little bit as we move ahead of depriving the enemy of his freedom of action let's go to the next page 0310 the next page which is 3-4. This notes that: "The enemy can also be fixed by a combination of methods which deny him information, deny him the ability to pass orders, and inhibit their execution. The enemy's information sources and his command system are central to his ability to concentrate force." Now, taking this out to a little bit more specific terms, one of the methodologies to fix the enemy - and when I say fix the enemy your description is depriving his freedom of action - is either -- is neutralising or destroying his ability to communicate. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well you say neutralising and destroying, but there might be other means, which you suggested here is -- is interfering in the electromagnetic spectrum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, the question was not whether this is the way to do it. But whether it was one of - as Mr. Kehoe said - methodologies I take it that he wanted to refer to methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of -- to fix the enemy, if you neutralise or destroy his ability to communicate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's one of the methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Russo, is there any dispute about --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- such a thing? Mr. Kehoe, is there any source which would even challenge that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's -- it's putting this -- first of all making a record here, Judge, of exactly how we're building up to the attack on Knin which is coming. I will move through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was waiting impatiently to understand where you would make what point. Please proceed, and don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- delay for us to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what your point is, because we usually - at least I hope - we're focussing on understanding the points that you want to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I can turn to page 2-7 of D1254 and we talk a little bit about disruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I just want to highlight this without bringing it to your attention. We will go through some of these items on disruption and on page 230 at the bottom of that, after dislocation: "Selective disruption can be used to break and confuse those assets that are crucial [sic] to the employment and coherence of an enemy's fighting power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm reading critical, but if you want to make it crucial then -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Critical. "Critical to the employment and coherence of the enemy's fighting power. It aims to rupture the integrity of an enemy's force and render him incapable of deciding and acting purposefully. The identification of those assets whose destruction is most likely to disrupt these enemy may not be easy. Military targets might include communication networks, command centres, transportation nodes, or logistic facilities." So when we're talking about the dislocation and disruption we are actually using these concepts in tandem and in this particular paragraph we talk about disruption by once again attacking communication facilities. Do these items go in tandem -- can they go in tandem during an offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly will be approached in an combined manner. All these are aspects like preemption, dislocation, disruption, are factors that a commander takes into account so there will be -- everything in a military plan will be in an combined manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a commander may have the option to attack these facilities with an attempt to disrupt and dislocate at a place well in depth away from the front line --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also talk in your report a little bit about simultaneous actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can stay on this report and go to page 2-9, 0235. I'm not going to read this whole matter, but the third sentence in, "By acting simultaneously": "By acting simultaneously against several levels of command the effect of cohesion is cumulative."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So is one of the options that we're talking about here, Colonel, not only hitting front line positions but also, for instance, communications centres or headquarters or logistics supply locations that may be well in depth and away from the front line in the way to have this cumulative effect against the enemy?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now lastly before we actually move to Knin, I just want to talk to you about the effectiveness of fire-power in the scheme here and going to paragraph 233 of the prior page, 2-8, of D1254. "Fire power," excuse me, paragraph 0233 on 2-8: "Fire pour destroys, neutralises, suppresses, demoralises and influences. It can be delivered by sea, land, and air platforms. It has physical, psychological and physiological effects. Fire-power provides the force to amplify or enable the effects of tempo, simultaneity and surprise. Its effectiveness depends on its volume, accuracy, and its suddenness and predictability [sic]." One again in using the combination --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could interrupt, for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I urge everyone, not you, primarily, at this moment, Mr. Russo, to slow down. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Apologies. I thought Mr. Kehoe had read predictability. It is now says unpredictability which is actually which on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Colonel, putting these concepts together and we're talking about an option on the table for the commander is to use a possible action, use a shock action, followed by -- after the shock action some artillery to disrupt and dislocate and to conduct and use artillery in that manner in a very sudden and unpredictable way to destroy the will power of the enemy. Is that a short synopsis of the items we just read? It's just one of the methods that a commander could employee.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But now you take some words out of this special paragraph of 233, and before I say whether this is an option yes or no you have to read that as well. Because I think that is quite honest and the sentence that I aim at is the psychological and physiological effects and of firepower are [indiscernible] and should be exploited by manoeuvre before they wear off because that is the combination of when you want to achieve something, either by shock action or by any action that you want to do, you have to see artillery or fire support in direct combination with manoeuvre in order to reach its effects that you want to have. That's what I want to highlight in my answer. And if you take that all combined then the combination of manoeuvre and fire-power is a -- is one of the possibilities, of course, that a commander can take into consideration to achieve his end state or his objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just staying with the manoeuvres. Were you told by the OTP that there were no -- there were manoeuvres or were not manoeuvres by the HV on the 4th? What were you told about infantry manoeuvres on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information given to me was that on the 4th they were in the proximity of Knin or inside Knin were no manoeuvres of infantry of HV. There were of course manoeuvres in the front line on the moment that the attacks started. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get into that, then. Now before we go to actual Knin, let me turn our attention to the next aspect here in D1247. And if we could go to 4-16, which is 1D65-0217, at the bottom of that page. In the operational ideas in the last sentence there: "The key to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you provide us with a page with a code which is not on the hard copy, but you do not provide us with the paragraph you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 0434, operational ideas at the bottom, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 0434, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last sentence there: "The key to operational art is to identify beforehand" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "What is going to be decisive in bringing about the down fall of the adversary. Identifying that decisive act comes from an analysis of COG." And the COG is the centre of gravity. We get that acronym from the prior page. Now, just putting D117 on the screen just briefly, D117, second page. In the upper right-hand corner -- excuse me, I think it's at the bottom -- or the centre middle column. Centre of gravity. "Centre of gravity, the NATO definition of the centre of gravity is the characteristics, capabilities, or locations from which a nation or alliance a military force or other grouping derives its freedom of action, physical strength, or will to fight." You're familiar with that are you not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And NATO doctrine upon many other aspects but NATO doctrine uses the centre of gravity as the basis upon which military campaign plans are built, don't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only military campaign plans. Centre of gravity is also used for defining where the political and state should be, so the centre of gravity can very well be a combination of political strategic level, and inside the military operation there is the commander designates a centre of gravity for his own forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The general idea in NATO doctrine, Colonel, is that the neutralisation and/or destruction of enemy's centre of gravity leads to the destruction and cohesion of the enemy to fight. That is the idea, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you again talk about only about neutralisation and destruction, and I cannot stress enough that that is only part of the solution. You can aim at an enemy centre of gravity in another way, even with diplomacy, so I -- I hate to repeat myself over and over again. But the words to be used is not only neutralisation and destruction because neutralisation and destruction are words that have a very physical sound even currently nowadays in NATO. That means the use of physical means and that's absolutely not the idea behind the books that have been written and that are now subject of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So just adding diplomacy to the area -- to the discussion --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only diplomacy, I'm sorry that I interfere. But there are all the means that a coalition has, the comprehensive means, the comprehensive approach are not limited to diplomacy or military means. The economical, political, informational, social that are all the parts that can you use in order to -- to influence the centre of gravity of any party, opponent, or actor in a conflict. I just want to be very specific and clear because you are only focussing on the words neutralise and destruction and to my opinion that doesn't give the correct overview that we are discussing about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, assume we're in a war situation, assume that we are planning to fight against the enemy that a war has been ongoing for several years. As a NATO officer, you want to determine what the centre of gravity is for your enemy, and you want to defeat your enemy and as a way of defeating that enemy you want to take out in some fashion the centre of gravity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You want to take out in some fashion the centre of gravity of your opponent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go with NATO doctrine yet further on the centre of gravity and staying with 1D1247. Mr. President, it's the next paragraph. It it's the next page 0434 -- it goes into centre of gravity analysis of 1247. I'm looking at the next page actually which is 1D65-0218. Now, this goes to the centre of gravity analysis and I want to go about the middle of that page where it says -- the paragraph actually where it sayings: "It is possible." Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "It is possible that at strategic level the COG may be something physical but it is more likely to be a morale entity related to a leader, a ruling elite, or strong-willed population. It is an adversary's morale strength to resist the alliance's end state and such morale resistance needs to be undermined neutralised or defeated for a lasting peace." Now, in this particular situation, Colonel, and you knew from reading the operation orders that the idea of the attack on Knin was the reintegration or the attack in the Krajina was the reintegration of the Krajina into the Republic of Croatia. In this context, the centre of gravity in this context for the ARSK was Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been reading that the order, the operational order read that the forces had to take control of Knin and the environment of Knin, and you may come to the conclusion that that is a centre of gravity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you came to that conclusion as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about the actual operation itself, and I'm interested in your analysis of the particular operation. And with the -- knowing that the Knin was the centre of gravity, you would have planned unquestionably that Knin was -- should have been taken in some fashion; is that not correct? In order for the HV to succeed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure, because taking control of Knin can, of course, mean various things. I haven't seen in that document what -- what the effect would -- would be -- what the effect would be that -- that would be needed. When you talk about an a populated area, an urbanised area, I fully understand that control only can take place when you have actual your own forces on -- on the spot, on the scene. So I understand that troops will be sent or would be sent to Knin in order to take control of that city. That's absolutely clear to me. It is only the doubt that I have is in which way you -- can you do that in which way you take control -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, carefully looking at the question it says, You would have planned unquestionably that Knin should have been taken in some fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question leaves it entirely open in what way and you're know explaining there are many ways of doing it which I understand to be a simple yes to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning to your report and this is it your addendum, P1260, that you note in paragraph 1 a that in order to be able to answer the questions of the Office of the Prosecutor an analysis of the information inserted in Annex A is made in the same way an intelligence officer, S-2 of a formation, brigade, battle group would use such information to sketch the situation of the enemy opponent forces and the environment they are operating in. The S-2 analysis is followed by an analysis of the own situation executed by the operations officer, the S-3. So I take it, Colonel, that when you were going through your analysis you analysed the entire combat situation from both sides of the equation; is that right both the ARSK and the HV side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I analysed both sides of the situation with the help of the information that was given me by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in the information of the OTP, did you come to understand the breadth of Operation Storm and the geographic area that it was in encompassing?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have -- I got an idea from that. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is that idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well the overall action, the overall Operation Storm was an operation as you already said to re-gain the country of the Krajina and it was done through various axis. There were as I recall there were I think three axes that the Croatian forces would say do their attack. And one of these axis was from Bosko - I cannot recall the name anymore - up to Krajina and from there I started concentrating on the action that taken against Knin specifically the artillery operation against Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you talked about the one axis. Where are the other two axes?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have the papers in front of me because then I can point out what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher can we provide the -- I take it from your report, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I refer to the operational order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're referring to P1125?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can bring that up on the screen. If we can bring P1125 on the screen. If we can go to the next page. And the next page, please. Apologies. Another page after that. I'm looking for the first page. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I take it that this is the document that you are talk about?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think so. I would prefer to have some time to read that carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And we can give you time at the break with the permission of Mr. President, if he wants to take a look at it further. I can continue to ask questions. Now, that the three axes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness needs to read it for answering the next questions, of course, of which we do not know yet what they are then, of course, he is entitled to read it again. If he doesn't need this information then he's invited to re-read the offensive operation order during the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I turn to page 5 of this document or two more pages in and scroll up just a little bit. Are those the axes that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that are the axes I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were analysing the actual facts concerning Operation Storm you were only dealing with these three axes?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this operational document and from the questions asked to me by the OTP, I have taken the step to focus myself on the axis Bosansko Grahovo-Knin and then specified on the questions asked by OTP on the use of artillery in Knin that is my ultimate -- my ultimate focus because that is my speciality that is the reason why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you review documents or information concerning the activity -- activities, that were taking place in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a map that was provided by the Prosecutor, 65 ter 4898. And my apologies, Colonel, sometimes it takes a little bit of time to bring these maps up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like you to take a look at this document. This is a document that has some broad strokes about the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can scroll up, please. Stop please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see Knin at the bottom. And as we scroll up yet further, we can see any number of items of offensive activity going on up through Sector North. Now, when you were doing your analysis of whether or not it was necessary to attack Knin, I take it from your answer that you did not factor in the fighting that was taking place in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have studied that because I was asked by the OTP to focus on the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you do know that -- I think you mentioned yesterday you had some degree of training in Warsaw Pact doctrine which you equated to JNA doctrine and you do know that the entire staff or the Main Staff or the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was being commanded from Knin. You know that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in neutralising and destroying the centre of gravity in Knin, you would agree that you are affecting not only the fighting that is taking place in the immediate geographic area of Knin but also the area in Sector North where fighting was taking place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be a fair possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This would certainly increase the necessity or the importance of neutralising the ARSK headquarters within the centre of gravity, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have nothing said against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My only thing is you didn't analyse this entire operation on Knin with this broader perspective in mind, did you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with respect to the fact that -- that there was a complete operation -- no, I realised -- I realised, of course, there was a complete Operation Storm going on, and I have stated that the -- the fact that there is an RSK headquarters and a president's office inside the city of Knin are important factors. I don't deny that. That's very valid and I have said they will be designated to be high value targets and high payoff targets. That is it something that I don't deny. You're absolutely right in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if during the attack communications at the ARSK headquarters are damaged, destroyed or compromised it would affect the theatre of operations into Sector North, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the whole organisation. I assume that -- that every army has its possibilities to de-route its communications and have alternative communications once you take out certain of the important points. So there would be alternative means. I would not compare communication means directly with an RSK HQ or a president's office. They are two different things, different in importance. So a military communication centre - and I stress the word military - if you take out, the military communications centre, it, of course, has its results for the operation, a negative result for an operation. But I'm convinced that as we have that any -- every army has alternative means to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just taking your answer that there are alternative ways to communicate, as a commander, you would not only want to take out the primary method to communicate or any -- you would also want to take out any alternative ways to communicate, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If, provided what I said before, that they -- that you aim yourself at the military means of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question on this, Colonel. You know based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know based on your training that the JNA trains their officers in their headquarters to direct operations throughout the theatres of operation, don't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what every headquarters does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you would conclude that maybe like -- unlike other armies, in an ARSK situation, destroying the communications of the ARSK headquarters is absolutely crucial to the ability of the ARSK to successfully conduct operations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, destroying a headquarters or destroying the communications of a military headquarters is crucial to an operation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I'll offer 65 ter 4898 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spent some time this morning and yesterday on doctrine simply because the first part of the report that Colonel Konings gave was just on doctrine in general and tried to flesh that out a bit. I will be turning to the actual battle that began on the 4th in the next session I would take it, but I wanted to give Mr. President, you, a road map of where I have come from and where I intend do move into right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber was informed that you had no objections against the admission of P1277 and under those circumstances and since you're not contradicting P1277, it's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And yes, Mr. President, that's right. My apologies for not doing it over night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't need to go to it, but what I'd like to explore is the statement in your report on page 43 a of 1259. There are no separate artillery operation. Fire support is an integral part of every operation and therefore taken into account in the decision-making process and the supporting targeting process. I would first like to bring up P1274, which is the map that -- I believe was discussed yesterday with Mr. Russo. And, Colonel, this is the map provided by the Office of the Prosecutor that has various targets located throughout the terrain. Yesterday we talked about the spots that are in and around Knin on the lower left-hand version. You see that in the middle of the page. And what I'd like to do is talk about the entire map. This is an artillery map -- or a map that shows artillery locations - and if we can scroll up a little bit - well in addition to those around Knin, does it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to 1D65-0484.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a 11-page document that we will be referring to at various times. I'm not sure how long it will take to come up, but it may take just a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Colonel, just to give you reference points what we have done here on this map is take P274 and lay it on a topographical map.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume with P247, you mean the map that you showed me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: P1274 was the initial map that you discussed yesterday with Mr. Russo and we just had on the screen.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we've taken the liberty in this particular situation to lay 1274 over a topographical map. I'm just trying to explain to you exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just ask you then, Mr. Kehoe, the map that was shown, the artillery map, seems to be an a 90-degree projection was that one adapted to what seems to be not the normal projection is that adapted in any way or ... just trying to understand what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it stretched as well or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were both -- the first map was, of course, on a topographical map as well, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do you understand what I mean. It seems that you're looking at the terrain -- the coloured one not the map part under a certain angle, which means that you get some - how do you say it? - it is stretched more or less. I don't know what technique you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that are you correct, Mr. President. I do believe what we have attempted to do is in conjunction some other documents taking these features. For instance, the red dots now portray these squares that were on the other map and to the extent there is any difference between the two, I think we can be adjusted or corrected, if you will, based on those particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking any corrections. I just would like to understand what I'm looking at, and maps, Mr. Misetic, I do understand that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What this is, is the map has been somewhat stretched points. The points on the two-dimensional map, you can see the red dots were then found exactly on the three-dimensional map and plotted exactly on to a three-dimensional map as they appear on the two-dimension map in order to accurately make sure that in fact it is stretched as necessary so that all the peaks are accurately depicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks as a fine result. I'm just wondering, maps and pictures in which the terrain was stretched I always want to know that we are talking about the same and that the combination is accurate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this particular map, Colonel, all we did was take the squares out, the artillery squares out and put dots on them so we could readily see them on the various features geographically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just go to the next page. This is the actual targets, with the idea that you can better able -- better see the topography of the area where the targets were. Again the frame of reference the Knin targets are down in the lower corner, and the ones up in the Dinara of course are towards the centre of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were going through your considerations and coming to your conclusions did you consider the topography in the area when you were analysing it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been shortly watching the topography yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, of course, we said previously that that is a significant item when a military commander is making a decision how he is going to deploy his forces and what the terrain is like?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Weather and terrain are two very crucial factors in analysing the upcoming operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4 in this, and we'll get into some of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I put one further question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because I want to understand what I'm looking at. There is in the original map, there is a distinction between the squares and the rectangles of approximately half the size of the square. That's not reflected, and I haven't got the translation here anymore about the agenda, but ... I get them now whether squares or whether rectangles, I get them as dots without any further distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing we were trying to depict there are locations of where the artillery attack was aimed, and we will get into the -- some of the reasons for that as we move forward. What we are trying to engulf is this, is the broader perspective of this attack it being in several different locations in addition to being some shelling in Knin. What we're trying to do, Mr. President, especially when it comes to these mountain peaks was getting some general areas as opposed to specific targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this -- this next map, Colonel, is the actual movement of the 7th Guards Brigade on the morning of the 4th. And again, Mr. President, this is a document received from the Office of the Prosecutor and as we can see below the overlay -- excuse me, the original map is ERN 0614-2289 which was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecutor and, of course, we can put that into evidence independently as well. Now, Colonel, when the artillery attack -- when the attack ensued on the morning of the 4th, you do know that the actual targets and the artillery was fired on multiple positions against the ARSK on the Dinara further in depth as well as firing on Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as we move up the Dinara, that -- those were the -- that was, in fact, the confrontation line between the HV and the ARSK, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So we can get this and I know we just talked about firing on Knin but I want to talk you about artillery fire on the confrontation line, on a reserve line, and in Knin all going on at the same time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's look a bit about what they were facing, and they being the HV. And we're talking about the 7th Guards Brigade, and this map that is depicted in the 7th Guards Brigade. The first goal of the 7th Guards Brigade was to attack after -- attack and take two very crucial mountain peaks, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that artillery was -- or fire was put upon those mountain peaks prior to or simultaneous with the advance, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you a little bit about a document you reviewed as we're going through this and that would be the operational diary. You did review the Split operational diary during the course of your review of -- or writing your addendum. I'm not sure you did it in the first one, but certainly you -- actually you had prior to the first one. Appendix B to the addendum reflects that you received the Split Military District diary on 8 December 2006. I'm sure that's about right, but you did review that diary?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I cannot recall that precisely. I have got the document and I have used it but -- but reviewing is a large word. I have used elements of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, it is important -- it's important to -- when you're getting a look at what is going on during the course of a battle to get a view from the Split Military District level, what they're trying to do, and what they're trying to attack as the day goes on; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next -- excuse me. The next slide here and we're talking about again the 7th Guards Brigade again on their efforts on the morning of the 4th, and if I may. Do you recall from reading the Split Military District diary which mountain peaks that the HV were trying to take first?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that without having any document in front of me. That's too long ago. I don't know the mountain peaks. I follow you in your whole approach, knowing the general idea, but I cannot recall any mountain name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Then maybe it might be easier just to go back to the diary and we will go back to the document that's on the screen to the extent that the diary can assist us with names and then we can go back and put them on places in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could just go back to the Split Operational -- Split Military District war diary or operational diary, P71, P71 -- no, no. We've got to tender it. And I'm looking for page 80 of 185. No? Excuse me, I stand corrected. It is 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm told by courtroom deputy -- courtroom manager that it is page 40 in the B/C/S. And, Colonel, bear with me, what I'm trying to do as we go into this is put the artillery attacks and the infantry attacks together as you suggest should be done in your report. I'm interested in the -- it is the next column over to the right. Okay. And that is for -- okay. If we go to the top of that page we can see the actual date. It should be -- see the date there is it 4 August 1995. And if we go at 0500, you understood from reviewing this that the fire began for attacks by the 7th Guards Brigade at 5.00 a.m. Let's go down to the next -- two more pages in this document, at the 0555 hours. And that should be in the left-hand column. That's 79 in the English and 42 in the B/C/S. If we go to 0555, "Intelligence reports are reflects Chetniks," - that is the word for Serbs - "reporting their positions on Dinara are broken through. Orders to intensify pace of 7th Guards Brigade and TRS-3." When you read that you understood that the artillery attack had preceded an infantry attack that commenced at 5.00, and, at the same time that the initial shelling was taking place in Knin. Is that clear in your mind that that is what was going on between 0500 and 055 [sic] on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite clear that those aspects happened although I haven't studied the operations of the 7th Guards Brigade in detail and I have not studied everything single detail in this diary of 150 pages, but I understand fully that this operation started on various places in trying to breach through a defensive line by using manoeuvre and artillery. That is absolutely understandable, and I understand also that the attempt was done to use artillery in a form of -- let's say, let's put it in a form of support -- of deep operation. Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you likewise come to understand that -- that on the 4th, of the movements of the 7th Guards Brigade were crucial to the success of the HV operations on that day?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether that was my memory of that. But I understand that the focus was lying on the movement of the 7th Guards Brigade during that morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, sir, the Office of the Prosecutor put your focus on the 4th Guards Brigade, didn't they, and not the 7th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The actual question from the OTP was to me to provide information on the use of artillery inside the city of Knin and general -- general background on the use of artillery in general. And by that, I have been focussed on the operation of the 4th Guards Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you come to learn that the crucial infantry ground manoeuvres were completed by the 7th Guards Brigade and not the 4th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's depending on which phase of the operation you're looking at, because if you focus on the 4th Guards Brigade, then that phase of the operations was crucial for the 4th Guards Brigade. So you cannot say that something is crucial because an operation may well be faced, and I have been reading that 4th Guards Brigade was -- was ordered to focus on taking control of Knin. So in order to do that, that seems to be a very important phase as well, so I do not deny that the actions of the 7th Guards Brigade were crucial in the total operation, but I do -- I'm convinced of the fact that the actions of the 4th Guards Brigade were as crucial as that. Because of -- that they had to take control of the city of Knin as we are all aware of that that was one of the most important things to achieve during the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the role of the 4th Guards Brigade at 0500 on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own area of operations in dong the first part of the attacks and later on they would be relieved in order to be able to take control of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did the 4th Guards Brigade attack on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
