utterances.text: I don't know that from detail, so you should -- I should have the operational order in front of me in order to be able to do that because you can reference to all the paperwork, and I don't have that in front of me. And I don't like to -- to recall all these details just purely from my head. So I would prefer if we talk about that, about task of the 4th Guards Brigade or the 7th Guards Brigade that I am able to have this operational order and to trade carefully because analysing an operational order is not something that you do purely from your head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know which units first broke through the ARSK lines on the 4th, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know which unit first entered Knin on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was elements of the 4th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The evidence that we have here, sir, is the 7th Guards Brigade that entered first on the morning of the 4th, the 5th not --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not the 4th Guards Brigade. Let us stay with this document and going to 0625 hours. That would be, 6.25, excuse me. That would be ... TS-3 says: "The 7th Guards Brigade requests support for the area of Pasalic Staja." And that is approved with Howitzer 155. Do you know where that location is, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we noted before that at least this activity that we're talking about shell activity, military activity, according to war diary we just read through 6.25 and obviously there's more entities going down. 6.40 notes: "The Chetnik noticed our Howitzers in the area of Vedro Polje?" I would like to talk to you what is going on back in Knin, if I may, while the shelling is taking place; and if I could bring up 65 ter 4518. Now, sir, this is it a report of an intercept that was taken by the -- or made by the Croatian authorities, as you can see, an intelligence report. It's dated 4 August 1995. And if we can go to the second page in the English. It discusses a conversation that was intercepted from someone in President Milan Martic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes: "From 0650 to 0705, a person named Dusko makes several private phone [sic] calls from the Martic office and says HV have pounded all the major towns and Knin is burning. He says that he is the only person on duty and that everyone else is in shelters or at home. He adds that nobody has arrived yet." Now, obviously the attack from what we've seen in the Split Military District diary and all the testimony to date commenced at 0500, and two hours into the attack, there is still no one at President Martic's or one person, excuse me, Mr. Dusko whoever he is, Dusko, is only one person at headquarters and certainly not President Martic. Now, you would agree that given the fact that there was artillery fire coming into Knin at this time, it's certainly, as a military officer, you could conclude that that artillery fire curtailed the movement and operation of -- of a very significant person to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Milan Martic, who was, of course, the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's your conclusion. I don't see that -- I don't see the correctness of that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, how would you conclude?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know whether the president was present in the city itself. So in general you speak with the statement of one person, that everyone is in shelter or is at home. Okay, that is fine. But it doesn't say anything about the presence of the president, yes or no. I don't know that. That's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Assume, Colonel, that Milan Martic was in Knin on the morning of the 4th, 1995 [sic]. Assume that.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fire by the HV on targets in Knin commences at 0500. Two hours into the operation, the Commander-in-Chief is not at his headquarters. You, as a military officer, could conclude based on that, that that fire had the effect of suppressing movements of a very important RSK official. Could you not conclude that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you assume that what you state that he is there, the suppressing fire probably will have excluded a lot -- the most, the bigger parts of the movements, yes, that's true. Okay, I'll leave it at that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that suppression of movement would bring with it a significant military advantage to the HV, at least for that two hours where the Commander-in-Chief could possibly not be found, or was as Duskan says in shelters or at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm going to be the question. I believe the document simply indicates that the president is not where Dusko is in the president's office. Mr. Kehoe asked the question about the Commander-in-Chief not being in his HQ. We all know from the other evidence that this is an HQ which is not the president's office and this document doesn't indicated whether he is there or where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are -- in the answers, and that's not for the first time that this happens, it is clear from the description of certain circumstances that a potential effect would be A, B, C, or D. Now what you are asking the witness, Mr. Kehoe, is on the basis of the assumption whether that would be the effect, yes or no. I think that hardly anyone would deny that if you are pounding town that people would be affected in their freedom of movement apart from what -- I would say it is to some extent common knowledge and then we add a lot of hypothetical data and if Mr. A would have been in town would have affected his freedom of movement as well, most likely yes, of course, if it has the potential why not against Mr. A, unless there is a good reason to consider him to be an exception. It's -- your point is clear. You deduce from this document where apparently the witness has no additional personal --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- observation about what happened or he can't add anything about the factual circumstances. This is a conclusion you consider reasonable to draw from that and you're inviting Mr. Konings to do that. As far as we're talking about potential, fine, no problem. Whether it affected or did not affect of course therefore you need to know more factual information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point is clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My issue is, of course, is that the direct examination was hypotheticals and I was presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're perfectly right in that -- that that's certainly not a strong point in the examination-in-chief. Now, whether it becomes any better to repeat that in cross-examination is -- well, at least could be subject for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- debate, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, at this time, I'll offer into evidence 65 ter 4518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objections Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hard to believe I couldn't be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this general time-frame, sir, and I'd like to show you another intelligence intercept, 1D65-0272. This is it another intercept from the 4th of August, 1995, Colonel, by Croatian intelligence service. It's involving several people but I'm most interested in talking about the intercept on the next page, where General Kovacevic is talking to Lieutenant-Colonel Radic, who is a commander of a battle group on the Dinara. And just as a time sequence, sir, this report was sent at 0830 on the 4th. And Kovacevic is talking to Radic: "Radic you can only come back dead. You must not come back if you leave your position. Here is trouble. They have hit the barracks (probably the Slavko Rodic barracks in Knin), they are shooting at everything and go eff yourself. Keep it in any way you can. You do not have another country by the great Serbia, and you eff their mother any way you know. I am telling you in Serbian. Go eff yourself, hold on my son, my falcon and this corps will progress once we have stabilised our state. Do [sic] you understand, you can only come back dead, you cannot come back alive?" Colonel you have been a military officer for a very long time. I think you would you agree that is not a very professional planner in which to address a subordinated, would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the way that other armies are dealing with their people. In my army that would not be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now do you know that General Kovacevic is a senior military officer in the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have seen his name, but I cannot recall that exactly on this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just assume that he was, for the sake of the next question and your reading this. If you were listening to this in real time, Colonel, would you have concluded, knowing what was going on in Knin, that this shelling had induced a level of panic in a -- in a senior military officer of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can come to the conclusion when you read this or when you hear that, but you take out one message of probably several ones, focussing on a certain issue, which seems to resemble a sort of -- which seems to -- to represent panic. But that might not be -- might not give directions to what will happen afterwards. I fully agree with that you that this reflects panic but it cannot directly be an indication -- one message cannot be an indication how a force will act later on, because for that you need a more deep-going analysis because one message is in itself is nothing. It -- it says something about the state of the mind of the general on that moment, on that moment in time; but there might be things happening later on, shortly after that might change it. I cannot judge a total situation on one message of one general telling very nasty things to one of his lieutenant-colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I'll offer into evidence 1D65-0272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1257 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to another item on this score, and if we could go to D930 in evidence. If we can just show the first sheet -- first page. Mr. Vrcalj is a -- if I can just go to the first page, first and so the witness can just get a frame of reference for this document. Thank you very much. Mr. Vrcalj was a senior officer again with the ARSK, and he writes about this incident as well as others; and I would like to turn page 7 of this document. And focussing towards the top of that page. I'm sorry, one more page. Towards the top of that page, first paragraph there. We jumped -- can you read that okay, Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "We [sic] jumped over the fence in a casern," which is the barracks, sir, "and entered the building where I worked up until four months ago. My Holster had been broken and I had given it to be resewn, so I came to reclaim it. The shells were landing in the casern. However, one needed to be particularly lucky for them to fall on your head. I asked the people present there if there were any volunteers to take me to the GS, the main headquarters. Nobody wanted. They didn't have courage or didn't want to gamble with their lives." Now, just by frame of reference, Mr. Vrcalj was the highest ranking artillery officer of the ARSK and based on some of the doctrine and some of the items that we have been speaking about this morning, would you agree with me that shelling by the HV would want to induce this type of fear by people such that it would suppress their movement. Here we have nobody wanting to go take General Vrcalj back down to the headquarters. That is, in fact, a goal that you would want to achieve, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general spoken is the use of artillery fire is bringing, denying your movement is bring fear in order to do things which are in an unprotected area. I think that is a normal human thing to want to do when projectiles are falling around you, to try to protect yourself and not to move, if not necessary. Although for soldier it might be necessary to get out and do their job. That's something that is needed to be done. But I do like to stress that the same effects occur against civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, taking this particular incident, you would agree that suppressing movement of soldiers by artillery fire would be to the military advantage of, in this case, the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a very broad conclusion that you take now because that has to be connected to the military value of the targets that you're aiming at because I can hardly imagine that -- let's assume that the military targets inside Knin were of low military value as is my conclusion in my report based on the information that was given to me, I can hardly assume that -- well, I cannot find the right word, I'm sorry about. That that limiting or even prohibiting the movement of those very low-value military units inside Knin would be of any military advantage at all of the whole -- of the Croatian operation. That's what I -- the connection between that, I cannot make. In general spoken, you are right. When you are able to prohibit movement of troops, then you will -- that can be of advantage but then those troops have to bring something to the battlefield. If you were talking in this case about prohibiting reserves, and then I mean real reserves like combat, troops, to be -- to prohibit them their movement to the front line, where the 7th Guards Brigade was making its move and where the 7th Guards Brigade was pushing forward in order to stop that, that movement, then I think you will have a very good point. But as I know that -- or let's assume that the information given by the OTP is the correct information, the military value of the targets in there, in Knin, I cannot see the military advantage of that. And then we come back to the point of proportionality, the value of targets, and the risk for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, you earlier said that you could hardly assume and then you said you couldn't find the word. If I can assist you. I don't know whether you explained it or whether how important it is. If you'd like to use that word in your own language I can see whether I assist you. If you say, I explain sufficiently then we just move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said I cannot find the right word, then I used after that the word limiting or even prohibiting the movement. I was looking for the word prohibiting. I couldn't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did I hear you correctly that you didn't see any military logic of shelling the northern barracks. Is that what your statement is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I did say that I did not see the direct connection between the military targets inside the city of Knin because of their low value, and the operation as a whole, in reaching military advantage through stopping the movement of those troops inside Knin by using artillery. That's what I said, and part of that is, of course, the shelling of the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 7th Krajina Corps was up on it's front line in the Dinara, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was their headquarters in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to look at the list where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was in the northern barracks, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So the 7th Krajina Corps -- not -- not the ARSK Main Staff headquarters, the 7th Krajina Corps was fighting up on the Dinara against the HV had their headquarters in the northern barracks and is it your testimony here or your opinion here that there was no military advantage to be gained by attacking the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm going make an objection, Mr. President. I think there's something that needs to be added to the question. The information that was provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually -- Mr. Russo, Mr. Russo. I don't think that objection against the question should be clear. If you say the question gives limited information and to that extent will lead the witness in a certain way then that may be true or not be true, but that is part, I would say of the latitude in cross-examination which is larger than -- and if there is anything you consider so important then we have to ask Mr. Konings to leave the courtroom to see whether -- because, of course, if there's -- if the question really is clearly misleading or -- then -- but then we have to discuss this in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think perhaps -- what I'm seeking is a clarification of the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if the Courts want to do that outside the presence of the witness then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question has been put to the witness. If he doesn't understand the question, we'll hear from him. If he gives an answer and if you have some doubts whether he has understood the question properly, you can further pursue this matter in re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. Perhaps it would be good to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 56, line 5. So the 7th Krajina Corps not the ARSK Main Staff headquarters, the 7th Krajina Corps was fighting up in the Dinara against the HV had their headquarter in the northern barracks; and is it your testimony here or opinion here that there was no military advantage to be gained by attacking the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's assume for the answer that -- the Krajina headquarters corps -- the headquarter of the Krajina Corps is there. I don't deny that a headquarter of a corps is a military target, and it is even a -- a very valuable military target. So if you attack the northern barracks in the assumption what you state that the headquarters is there, I can understand why you do that. The only thing I want to add to that is that we have discussed that before, seen the construction of a headquarters like it was stationed there, you can have serious doubts in the use of artillery in trying to take that headquarter out in such a way that it will be out of action. That is my -- my serious doubt about that. And, at the other hand, the information given to me was that the corps headquarters was -- that practically nobody was there. But that's -- I think up to you and to Mr. Russo to talk about that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the discussion we have here is one -- and your answer is one of proportionality and when you look at this on a proportionality scale your doctrine would dictate that you couldn't fire on the northern barracks under these circumstances. That's where you come out; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're misrepresenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm asking a question in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. You're summarising more or less the answer of the witness, and then I think you should at least include that rather important part of his answer was that an artillery attack would not be the appropriate means of firing at the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is part of the proportionality equation, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then make that part of your question. If you are summarising then you should do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your proportionality equation there could be decisions alter than absolute destruction. It could be a desire to suppress activity as we see in the paragraph on the page. There could be a desire to interdict activity or disrupt operations of the military. Those would not encounter or bring into bear destroying the building, but even with these ideas of just suppressing the activities of the ARSK in the northern barracks not destruction just suppressing activity you conclude on the proportionality scale that your doctrine would preclude or question an artillery attack on the northern barracks. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not accurate at all. I'm sorry to say that. What I tried to explain is that when you take the assumption that in the northern barracks is a fully operating headquarter of the 7th Corps, let's take that as an assumption, then the conclusion cannot be other than that, that is a valid military target of high priority, and the conclusion can be for a military commander or even for a -- a political decision that you want to take that headquarters out of action. You have various ways in doing that. That can be destruction, as you describe, that can be neutralisation, that can be interdiction. The only thing that I say is that achieving those as facts with artillery is not the most likely way because destruction is out of the question. Neutralisation is out of the question because you will not do any harm to the building. You may hope for interdiction or you may hope for psychological effects inside that headquarters, which may cause panic in that headquarter. That's up to -- and that depends on the information that you have on what is the morale of the people over there. That can differ from situation to situation. And then, of course, then comes into the proportionality and then, of course, comes into account the presence of the civilian population in that area. So there are numerous factors that you have to take into account in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Colonel. Let's move down on this page and just go to the next paragraph: "I entered the building and, boy, was there a lot for me to see [sic] two shells landed in the parking area between the buildings, exploded and destroyed the entire car park of the GS, the general headquarters. It must have been that one good artillery operator has stuck them precisely at that location." Had you reviewed this item at all prior to coming here today?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read this document. I don't know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us continue on, towards the bottom of the page: "I asked around ... the other commanding officers from the GS since they were not present. There were just a few of us. Some didn't report throughout the day although their sleeping quarters have been situated in the retirement home which was located some 400 metres away. They succumbed to fear. Inability of a commanding officers to react in hard situations had had," I'm reading directly, "had had to be revealed before, not there and then when those who were supposed to help others required helping themselves. A good part of them wasn't prepared for the war, neither physically nor psychologically." Now recognising that you had not read that before, Colonel, you would agree with me, based on what General Vrcalj, the senior artillery officer for the ARSK, notes in his book that the attack by the HV clearly succeeded in suppressing the activities of officers in the ARSK would you not conclude that from this?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not directly because what -- you come up with single statements from single people, which in itself might be correct, which might be wrong, I don't know. I haven't been reading them before. And it states also on some places that I ask around about the other commanding officers from the GS since they were not present. That doesn't say anything. That could also mean that the whole HQ was not manned properly and that they had reserve HQ somewhere in the field somewhere from where they were doing directions. Those statements here don't give me any direct lead into the fact that there was panic. I can assume there was panic. Of course, I can. But the conclusion that from this writer, and he might have been a high-ranking officer in the army, but they succumbed to fear and ability of commanding officers to react in hard situations had to be revealed before not there and then when those were who were supposed to help others. That could already mean that those people already were gone for a long period. So when you attack a headquarters and again I don't deny that that is not a military thing to do, then as an attacking force you have you to be sure, have you to be -- have you to have the information, what the -- the headquarters is doing, what is the real military value and what is are all the ins and outs around that headquarters. And such a single presentation of some sentences of an artillery chief of that army, okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if I can correct once I think you put a not in there and if you can look on the screen, starting on line 15: So when you attack the headquarters -- and, again, I don't deny that you say this is not a military thing to do, did you say it is a military thing to do?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a military thing to do, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just thought there was a not in there that was not supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have been -- you noted in the course of your testimony that you were told that the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps was not in the northern barracks. I would like you to take a look at D928, page 33. This is another book by another senior-ranking officer of the ARSK, General Sekulic. This is it 33 in the English, 38 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I may have missed it but you said in the course of your testimony that you were told that the headquarters were not in the northern barracks, could you give me the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can find it in a second. I heard it, Your Honour. I will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic apparently knows where to find it so that I can verify it. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking it up right now I am virtually certain he just said it within the last ten minutes but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour, and that was the information provided to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that is clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is General Sekulic's book, and if I can just go with the third paragraph in the second full paragraph the third paragraph down: Colonel Stevo Draskovic. Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel Stevo Draskovic, 7 Corps, it is actually 7 Dalmatian Corps, assistant commander for morale confirmed that the command post had been in the barracks, in the context, this is the northern barracks in th barracks in Knin until midnight on 4/5 August and was then moved to Padjene. Now the information that was given to you by the Office of the Prosecutor was given from that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to -- back to P71, which is the diary, Split Military District war diary, and going to page 79 in the English in that document and page 42 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can spin that, please. Going down to the bottom -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 7.45 at the bottom, HV artillery hit the barracks in Knin. So that is the kind of items that would you expect to be coming back to General Gotovina that his artillery is hitting what you even state is a military target, the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this particular point doesn't say me anything. Being a commanding general or an artillery commander, I immediately would go back to the source that gives me that information because there are various crucial factors misting. This only states that you hit the barracks, point, end of discussion; and what as a commander, I need to know, what are the effects that I have achieved what does that bring to my whole operation because building that operation is a continuous analysing of the things that are happening. So with all due respect, this type of reports doesn't say me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. Colonel, this is a war diary, isn't it? I mean it is actually --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Chronically events, not on a minute by minute basis but events that take place on regular intervals during the course of the battle to keep the commander up to date, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would have -- I with would have -- I except this kind of reports is underpinned by other reports where they say what the effects are that you achieve because that is what we're talking about here. We're not talking about the report system of an army or how a diary is built. I know very well what a diary is. But if you present me this and you ask my opinion about this diary, I say you, quite clear, this doesn't say me anything and I, as an artillery officer, as a commander, would like to -- I would expect to see also those documents or those radio communications that underpin what is happening here, because it doesn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, we're in the middle combat here. In addition to this particular piece of information you don't know what was told to General Gotovina at this time in conjunction with this, do you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is it crucial that you know that. It is crucial for a commanding officer once you attack a -- such apparent important headquarters because that's your -- that's the discussion that we have. The northern barracks were occupied by the headquarters of the 7th corps. And as assume that the headquarters was there because we were reading that in that book what you presented that they were there until the 5th in the morning so they were there. Let's assume that during the moment of the attack. If I would be a commanding officer of an attacking force I would be very interested and even if I would be the commander of the overall operation I would be very interested in knowing what the effect would be of the actions of my artillery in trying to take out that headquarters. And a diary, as is presented here, is not used for that. But I would be very interested in first of all what is the effect that you try to achieve by attacking that barracks, neutralisation, destruction, whatever and what is the effect that is done, what is the real effect. And so that that is crucial for the further -- the further overall operation, because what you stated is that, if this is a high priority target, the taking out of that high priority target will influence the whole operation, being a commander of an operation, I would like to know this at first what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's continue the time sequence, Colonel, this is at 7.45 and let's see what is reported back at 7.55 which is on the next column, if we can just shift is it over. Chetniks starting the counteroffensive in -- in defence of the area of the 81st Guards Battalion HV. 81st Guard Battalion informed. TRS-3 ready for support. Now you had this diary, and I am sure you read that. Tell us about this counteroffensive up by the Serbs and where it took place?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't read any single detail in this diary so I used it as a general background information, and I told you that this type of diary does not bring you so much information. But I didn't study the counteroffensive of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, when we are getting the lay of the battlefield and what is transpiring it is very important for you looking at this entire operation to understand what's transpiring on the battlefield not just in Knin but all the up to the Dinara on the confrontation line, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is part of it. I understand the general outlines of the operation. That's what was given to me. That's what I have been studying. The next step was to concentrate on the actions, specifically the actions by artillery that was taken towards Knin. I did not study every single counterattack of either -- of both parties. That was not requested to me by the OTP, so I did not do that. I know what the aim of Operation Storm is, was, and I focussed from there on the use of artillery against Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, sir, you said in your document that fire support is a integral part of every operation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you didn't study the infantry part of the operation but only studied the artillery part?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Explain please?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I focussed on the activities that were taken against Knin. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Up in the Dinara were you aware if casualties were being taken by the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throughout the diary, you -- you can read that there were casualties taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go down to 9.55 at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we're hearing this noise it is because the steps in front of the building are in need of repair and that is not pleasant but, just for you to explain that it nothing else and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Notes that helicopter for Piketa to collect there an is an illegible word and go to Veli Vrh to pick up casualties. Approved by General Gotovina. Now you noted -- that is one of the series of items where its described the casualties that the HV is taking during this fighting up in the Dinara, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your assessment in going through the documents was that the fighting on the Dinara was quite intense, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't deny that. I haven't been there, but I assume that breaking through a defence line takes casualties. That is unfortunately a part of a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go through the sequence of events as to what transpired thereafter, and if I may, if we can turn to D923, which is a document that is signed -- that is written by General Mrksic on the 26th of August, recounting the events of the day. If we can just go to the first sheet of that. I don't believe this is the correct document. D923, did I misspeak there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the correct document, D923. It's page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, Colonel, who General Mrksic is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall his name directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you can assume for the sake of this discussion that he is the senior commanding officer of the ARSK at this time.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Third paragraph in: "The Ustasha breakthrough over the Dinara mountains during the afternoon of the 4th of August represented the greatest threat for the collective activities of the 7th corps. The MUP special unit leaving its positions on the Dinara mountain [sic] around 11.00 offered the Ustasha forces a possibility for a swift break through over the Dinara -- over the Dinara mountains towards Crvena Zemlja. In that way the defence in the rest of the Dinara mountains and the dense of the 1st Light Brigade in the wider area of Vrlika were compromised. The appearances of the Ustashas in the area of Knin endangered the rear of the 7th Motorised Brigade and the defence of their [sic] Drnis axis?" First before we move of off this Colonel, were you aware that members of the Ministry of Interior, the MUP special unit that is described here, were operating in conjunction with the ARSK on the front line in the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that particular issue, if in fact they were -- and by the way this MUP special unit is police. There has been much evidence in here that the ARSK unit that was up there were policemen. So were you made aware that these policemen took on military roles at various times and in combat settings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this particular case. I know from my -- from the whole conflict in the Balkan in the 1990s that police forces were used in that role. But I'm not aware of this in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, assuming that the police officers became parts -- part of the ARSK during times of combat they would no longer have their civilian aspects but would become like any other soldier on the front line; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the specific legal arrangements about that. That is up to you to conclude. We don't know in my army the system of militarising police officers. We have military police. If these special forces, these special units were military police, then they are military. I'm not familiar with the system that you militarise civilian police officers for use inside the military organisation and what their rights and their constraints are in that case whether they can be used as full military forces. Again, in NATO, we have, in our country, we have military police officers and they are entitled -- they are acting as military forces but they are not used as combat forces whatsoever. They have special duties inside our army. So I cannot give you a proper answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You can assume for the sake of this discussion that this MUP special unit was a minister of the interior police force that was made part of the military. And you can also assume that this police force that was up on the front line were headquartered in the police station in Knin. Now, under those circumstances, where this police force was now a fighting force for the ARSK, their otherwise civilian police headquarters then becomes a military target, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you assume under those assumptions that you say, and if that's the regulation inside the ARSK, I don't know the legal side of that, it seems to be that they are part of the military, and for that reason a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's turn our attention to the sequence of events as they unfolded on the 4th with the 7th Guards Brigade and the ARSK, and to assist us in that, let us go back to P71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is 80 in the English and 43 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's in the second column, 12.55, yes, the column over. If we can go through these relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 12.55, 7th Guards Brigade reports that positions were taken in the Bancica [phoen], K6794240, Samar, Igla, Brezovac, Crnacka Draga [phoen]. Now, are you familiar with about those particular locations, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me give you a quick frame of reference then and go back to 1D65-0484, which is the map. And I'd like to go to page 5 of that document and focus on Samar and Igla. And if we can just -- I don't know if we can blow up the centre of that at all. Now you see those ridges, those two mountain points that are in there. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see many mountain points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the names S-a-m-a-r up at the top and I-g-l-a next to it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I-g-l-a is, if you go to Samar and you just move to the right. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the blue more or less Frank Tango [phoen] plate over it, it is on the left side, the left top side approximately in the middle you see Samar, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it Samar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and Igla is to the right of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now those two peaks are taken, it notes in the diary at 12.55. Let -- and we don't need to put this on the screen, but if I can just read it at a risk of not flipping back and forth too much and this is P71. The time entry on the 4th is 1330. It notes from the 7th Guards Brigade that the enemy first line broken enemy chaotically running away. 1445, 7th Guards Brigade notes seized Badanje and Visibaba. Now do you see those locations, the two that are directly in the centre of that page?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. These -- this -- these particular features, these features that we are talking about, the diary reflects took from 0500 in the morning until 1525 in the afternoon. Did you ask the OTP for any addition detail about the level of fighting that was taking place in order for the HV to successfully take these locations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would that not have been important for the greater upon text for you to understand what was going on in the entire battlefield and not just Knin but all the way up in the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I don't see the connection between this specific part of the battlefield in relation to the use of artillery in Knin because this is a -- I'm sorry, this is it a description of how on a part of the battlefield a battle unfolds, apparently very successful for the HV forces with the conclusion that the Serb forces are running away. In itself I don't see this is an direct connection between that and the -- the use of the artillery in the whole operation towards Knin. I think you can clarify that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before you consider whether or not to clarify, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a small procedural issue to deal with totally unrelated to this witness. Therefore, Mr. Konings, I will ask you already to leave the courtroom, escorted by Madam Usher when I raise this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were translations issues raised by both the Cermak and the Markac Defence. It was Mr. Kay and Mr. Kuzmanovic who dealt with it in relation to the Turkalj statements. It was then agreed that you would -- where an example was given only that you would give a list of your concerns to the Prosecution. Mr. Kuzmanovic joined in that exercise. The Prosecution would then look at it and we would hear whether there was any agreement on inaccuracies in the translation. We've not heard from the parties since then, and since the Chamber would very much want to avoid using material which is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We in fact sent our suggestions to the Prosecution several days ago and my understanding is that they're in fact reviewing it at the moment, and they will come back to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your honour, ours is expected to be ready by Monday to be sent to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I agree with all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree with all, yes. I don't think it makes much sense to first deal only with the Cermak inaccuracies and not to take them all together. The Chamber, of course, would like to resolve this, because we're working on the material as well, and we would like to know whether we are facing inaccuracies in the material which would, of course, stop us from further looking at. How long is your list, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My understanding is, Your Honour, is it is about four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four pages. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're looking at about the same amount. The only reason it is delayed for me is I need the audio transcript and it took a while for me to find our version of it because it was submitted to us last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could we invite the OTP to give full priority to verifying the complaints by Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said you expect to give it on Monday to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a first impression well, let's say, I was inclined to say next week, Wednesday, but we're not sitting on Wednesday. So next week Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We'll endeavour to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear from you. We will have a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, just looking at the map that's on the screen, and we talked about from the diary positions taking from Samar, Igla, Badanj, Visibaba, and we note the 7th Guards Brigade took those in the every afternoon of the 4th. And when you were looking at that, sir, you understood that there was a military logic to shell those spots prior to them actually being taken because they were in fact resistance points for the ARSK, were they not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You refer now to the hilltops that you were referring before -- before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the hilltops, and I'm referring to as we look at this map of the activities of the 7th Guards Brigade on the 4th, and we look at the dots which are the locations according to the map that the Prosecutor put into evidence were targets of artillery --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- you can in fact conclude that there was military logic behind hitting those locations with artillery. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That in itself is right. They seem to be part of a -- let's say defence line. I assume that they are all military targets, so this is an complete logic in doing manoeuvre and fire-power together in order to break a defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise as we go this map Pljesevica and Anica Glava obviously that had not been taken as of that day, those were likewise resistance points for the ARSK, and there was in fact military logic behind shelling those as well, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I only repeat there is a full military logic in the combination of the use of manoeuvre all types of fire-power in order to break a defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we look at the dots that were shown to you by the Prosecutor that we have just in this map there was a military logic to shell each one of these ARSK resistance points, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided they are military targets, then I don't think that there is any doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you check if they were?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't checked that. I haven't been asked to do that. As I told you I only have a rough overview of what the 7th Brigade did. I have not been tasked by the OTP to study the operations of the 7th Brigade with respect to these specific military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this was in fact the defence line for the town of Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's talk to yet another aspect of the shelling, and I'm interested in a couple of issues. We noted, and if we go back to P71, page 80. 80 of the English; 43 of the B/C/S. And if we can go to the right hand column please. These are the two entries we talking about just briefly prior to the break. More specifically, the one at 1330: "Enemy fire line broken. Enemy chaotically running away as reported by the 7th Guards Brigade at 1330." I want to bring up yet another document 1D65-0515. If we can spin that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, I don't have a B/C/S translation of this yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a B/C/S interview, Colonel, that -- I know that I said -- it was a B/C/S document that incorporates a Belgrade radio interview that notes at -- this is at 1300 Greenwich mean time which, of course, is 1500 in Knin at the time. And if we can just go down to General Mrksic talking at -- at 0500, we can see the comparison there with Greenwich meantime. "This morning, 4th August, the Croatian army attacked the Republic of Serbian Krajina by massively bombarding all populated places particularly Knin. The bombardment is still in progress our army is still firmly in control of the forward front line, the Croatian army was unable to seriously breach our like except on the route leaving from Grahovo to Cvrnje Smelje [phoen] to Knin." Now that's the line that we were talking about, Colonel, was it not 1330?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll to offer 1D65-0515 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1258 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, as a commander, and you are being informed that the enemy line is broken and that part of the enemy is chaotically running away, you as a commander would try to prevent them from going to a place where you didn't want them to go; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that might be a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's called shaping the battlefield, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is shaping the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- shaping the battlefield according to such requirements or such conditions that is in favour of your own operations. And, again, trying to -- well, I would expect in this -- no. Leave it at that. I assume have you a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do. Well, in shaping the battlefield, you as a commander, with -- giving orders to artillery asset, if you saw the enemy fleeing, and you wanted them to go right and to not go left, because it was to your military advantage, you would consider laying down fire in that left-hand location to prevent them from going there, wouldn't there -- wouldn't you.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's a possibility but I would not use my artillery alone for that because you need a combination again from manoeuvre and artillery in order to prevent completely what you went them to do because it is just not possible to move a whole force only with the use of artillery in a direction that you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's be broader then. You would use assets at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To convince them for own health and well-being that they better go right and not left?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just one of the possibilities that you have in a given scenario. That's up to a commander to decide, because if that happens when an enemy force is retreating from a defence line, a commanding officer of the attacking force has various possibilities and on the spot, he will analyse together with his staff the situation and will come up with a possible cause of action that can be -- that can be a combined course of action that does not necessarily mean only to be trying the enemy forces to go left or right. You can also try to stop them, but you can also take advantage of the situation in focussing your force on achieving the end goal that you want to achieve. You may decide even to leave the enemy where he is, let him flee, let him go, and I focus now, in this case on going towards Knin and trying to end the situation as soon as possible. So there are numerous possibilities of which the one that you describe makes part of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are multiple points.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I don't mean to preclude one as opposed to the other. But when you read this in your diary, did you ask the Prosecutor for any information as to where these enemies forces, these ARSK forces had run to?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to P1268 that was received in evidence yesterday. Now, the last entry there at 1500 you were asked questions about that by Mr. Russo, and it notes: At 1500 hours, in the time of General Mrksic's radio interview with Serb radio, Belgrade, D1258, there were -- in irregular intervals a total of 18 projectiles, T-130s in this instance, were fired from a T-130 at the general area of Knin. Now, when you were shown this document and you had the diary to review, did you ask the Prosecutor whether or not he had any information that these projectiles were being fired upon soldiers that were retreating back to Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that we had this type of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's assume for the sake of argument that they were in fact retreating back to Knin at 15 00. The firing of 18 T-130 projectiles in their direction would certainly deter these soldiers from coming into Knin, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. I don't think so. It depends on -- it is all assumption what are you doing now because how many soldiers were fleeing, how were these rounds used? It says at irregular intervals. It says at a T-130-millimetre. Was it a concentrated fully of more than one gun? Was it only one gun that fired single rounds somewhere in the terrain because the effect that you want to achieve is something that diminishes immediately because if the effect to be achieved, especially against soldiers that are in chaos or that are flee in the open is when you fire one or two rounds, they will be -- they are be scared. They will be able -- maybe casualties. But if these irregular intervals are taking more time, then they will coming together and they will have the opportunity to flee again because the effect of artillery is diminishing very fast very quickly. And I don't deny that even one round can bring -- can build up more chaos and more panic, but the information here, in this point, as I stated yesterday, doesn't say me anything about the use of this 18 rounds of -- a T-130 at the general area of Knin. To me, it is just a number of saying we fired 18 rounds somewhere. It is useless information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Let move on a little bit and let's move to the next day of the battle, and before we do that if we could go back -- I would put on the screen 1D65-0484, and if we could go to -- to number 5, map 5 in this scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we just blow that up a bit, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I should address you, I think. P1268, time in the original seems to be 2000 hours whereas in the English version it seems to be 2.00, 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we can correct that in the file in the amended translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this is again the situation based on the map that we looked at page P1274, do you know from reviewing of the documents that part of the goal for the 7th Guards Brigade was to take Pljesevica and Anica Glava but they were unsuccessful on the 4th because of pretty stern resistance by the ARSK. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not quite sure, so the answer is, on this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, okay. If we can move to the next slide. And before we do this, I mean -- again, I did talk about some of these other topics but, of course, if one of the goals for the 7th Guards Brigade on the 4th was to take Pljesevica and Anica Glava there were certain that those high ground features this certainly would have been military logic going for the shelling of those targets, wouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided they are military targets. I assume that you aim at that then shelling those targets is in itself no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's assume for the sake of this argument that in fact the line was stopped and -- well, it was a goal of the HV they failed to take Pljesevica and Anica Glava and let's move to the operations of the 4th. Than would be in the next map. Excuse me, I'm sorry, the 5th, my apologies. I'll saying the 5th of August. If we could have the next map up. Actually, two maps up. That's it. Now, Colonel, you talked to some degree about the advance on the 5th, and, Mr. President, what we have done in this point is to take two additional items that were provided to us by the Office of the Prosecutor and the underlying documents are an incorporation of the 7th Guards Brigade commander's decision map and that is reflected in blue; and the 4th Guards Brigade operations map which is reflected in pink. And, again, we have overlayed it on this topographical Google map. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kehoe, we are talking about artillery fire and targets and type of fire the coordination with ground manoeuvres but as I said before no distinction in your reflection has been made between, at least, we could ask the witness is described in different ways, the one being preparation fire and the other apparently -- well, at least not called preparation fire and from what I understood from Mr. Konings, preparation fire is to clear the ground so that ground troops can move forward. Now, that seems to me if we go into such detail as you do, to be something to also consider, so I'm a bit troubled by red dots, where we started with rectangular and squares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I did in this point and of course we can go back and bring in the rectangular square with the originals, Mr. President, what I was just attempting to do, what we are attempting to do at this point is going through the maps as provided by the Office of the Prosecutor showing these individual targets and the logic behind hitting these targets as it moves in conjunction with the infantry movement on the 7th and the 4th Guards Brigades because it directly bears on the Colonel's statements in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see what you do, but you are ignoring a distinction which is made in the original maps and especially with the last -- we, until now, we were dealing with -- I would say the rectangular targets and are coming close to or are already at the square ones which appear to be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can clarify with regard to those particular targets and the differences between those. We can certainly over the weekend clarify any points in that regard that the Chamber would like. For the purpose of just this, I just complete going through the next day with an effort just to show is there is a logic to using artillery generally be it T-130s or Howitzers or MRLs on these various locations. These were individual places that had been focussed upon by the 7th Guards Brigade and the 4th Guards Brigade and that there was a military logic by hitting these locations and that was the effort that I was trying to get through with the expert, because, of course, he reviewed these documented and he reviewed some of the background material as to these particular targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you repeatedly stressed how important it is for an expert to look at all the information available to him. What I see here in this exercise we are losing some information. I leave it to that at this moment. Mr. Konings, from my remarks you may be aware that the red dots on the original map do not all appear in a similar same and with similar agenda with it. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and we will put the actual underlying documents into evidence, Mr. President, which will reflect the rectangles and the squares, so there would be some clarity as to which is which.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning to the 5th, sir, and the 5th, as you know, was a joint operation with the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade with the 4th taking a flanking manoeuvre to the right, or, in this case, I believe it would be towards the north; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an order, 65 ter 2199, and then we can move back to the map. And -- this is an order of General Gotovina, 3 August 1995, and on the second page it notes the introduction of the 4th Guards Brigade to be given maximum fire support on the right flank. Had you seen this document prior to today?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have seen many documents, so it is hard for me to recall all of the documents that I have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I'll offer into evidence 65 ter 2199.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And can we go back again to 1D65-0484 which is at page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And again, sir, I would like to ask you, when you looked at this particular map and looked at the movements of the 7th Guards Brigade and the 4th Guards Brigade, did you discuss the strategy or did you analyse the strategy of hitting the various targets that we have before us in dots as part of the overall strategy of the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean we discussed? Discussed with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at this in a little bit more detail. When you look at these particular items that had been shelled according to the underlying maps, did you analyse the reasons why these items had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I analysed very briefly because my first job asked by the OTP was not focussing on the actions of all these brigades that you are presenting now but focussing on the actions that were done in -- in the preparation of taking and taking control of Knin and especially focussing on the use of artillery inside Knin. But, of course, I have had a general view, and I will not call it a complete analysis of the whole operation. I have created myself a general view of what happened, and when you see the actions develop as you present them here on the screen, I will not deny that this is, in itself, a regular, military operation, which under folds along certain lines, which unfolds partly as it was planned but which falls party as it wasn't planned. Because that is normal for a military operation when are you not able to break a defence, you take alternative action by flanking manoeuvres or whatsoever. So in that context, the red dots or the rectangulars that were presented are estimated being military targets and form part of the military potential of the force that is attacked. So for me there is no need to analysis that further and again I was not asked to analysis that further, and if you ask me to analysis all those single situations I only can say then have you to give me time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just said on page 85 at line 22: "My first job asked by the OTP was not focussing on all these brigades that are you presenting now but focussing on the actions that were done in preparation of and taking control of Knin." Now, how could you analyse information on the taking -- taking control of Knin without analysing the activities of the brigade that actually took over Knin, that being the 7th Guards Brigade? How could you do that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to you that I have a general overview of the operation as it run up until the moment that Knin was approached and from that moment on, I took my detail analyses on the facts that were given me by the OTP, which was the assumption about all the targets that were in Knin that we discussed before, and on the fact that there was the entering of Knin was only on the 5th of -- of August. And of course, I had a general idea about what was happening, but I have not analysed the whole operation in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just ask one simple question. Did the OTP tell you that it was the 4th Guards Brigade that took Knin on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to this and looking at the targets putting aside your discussion of Knin, the rest of the red dots, which are targets on the underlying map did you find any information to lead to you conclude there was not a logical reason for attacking all of these targets? And if so, what was the reason for not attacking them, if you found any?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no reason to doubt these targets. Because they are apparently in connection with defence forces. The things that I have doubt from the beginning on is those aspects in the order that were given in shelling cities, like Benkovac, like Knin. That is the problem that I raised in the discussion with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Colonel. We'll get to that. Let's go to the next slide and follow up -- focus a little bit more on the activities of the 5th. If we look at the activities of the 5th, sir, and this is a blow up of this map and the idea was to move to the Golubic depot as well as the railway station in Golubic. You can see in the dots as were it Crni Vrh. Now if we can go to -- actually we can stay here. With regard to the Golubic depot -- I mean are you familiar with the Golubic depot and exactly how large it was --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with how far away the Golubic supply depot was from the railway station?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the scale of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, putting aside the map. I'm talking about generally --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, then I have to guess, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No idea how far the ammunition depot is from the train station?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't guess about that so if you want me to give you that, I cannot recall that out of my head without having a proper map in front of me with where I can see the scale. I don't know from -- from my head all these single possible targets in one of the operations of one of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you familiar or given any information about munitions being taken from the Golubic depot and being brought to the Golubic railway station and being transported on the rail line between Golubic and Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how far Golubic is from Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I estimate it must be under ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So we're talking about a relatively short distance --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- to move things by rail?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next slide. Now, we can see the Golubic depot moving up to the left from the red dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next slide please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is again another set of maps that was put together from the items given to us -- to the Defence by the Prosecution. They are listed below. And it has targets of the ARSK, a junction, and Bulina Strana; and if I can just go to next page in this. Now, Bulina Strana, the shelling of Bulina Strana, were you given any information as to what the ARSK was using Bulina Strana for?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know that it was going to be used as a position to defend Knin on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 1D65-0484.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is that the Google Earth presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1260 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just staying with Bulina Strana, would it have been important for you to know that that is, in fact, a high ground feature that the ARSK was going to use for the defence of Knin in making a determination whether or not the shelling of that location was proper?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's valid information to have a that available, no problem about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you weren't given that information?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall that. I don't think so but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to some targets in Knin because I know that in your table on P260 [sic] and also in various commentary on documents presented by the Prosecution, you were asked about targeting and your specific opinions about various targets. And I would like to bring up the targets or the list of targets on P1271 that Mr. Russo discussed with you. Now, this is the -- you recall this document, Colonel, discussed with Mr. Russo and you were asked about the first entry, the church in Knin; and Mr. Russo at page 14434 at line 12 to 15 asked: "And I will ask you the same question, Colonel Konings, given your training and experience whether or not you believe it is appropriate to include a hospital, any hospital, on a target list." And your answer is: "No." Now, your answer was based on your belief, sir, that it was in fact a hospital at that location --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. That was the church, no, no, I'm sorry the ... Can we move down to ... there it is the hospital, the third from the bottom. Apologies. Not the church, see the hospital is the third from the bottom KV10, 710 I'm talking about the one that's at the bottom, Colonel, I was referring to the -- mistakenly the beginning one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that is what you were asked about by Mr. Russo and you gave the testimony that I just discussed.
